concept.name: Asian option
concept.definition: An exotic option whose payoff depends on the average price of the underlying asset during some portion of the life of the option, rather than on the underlying's price at a single date.
concept.intuition: An Asian option pays on the average price over time instead of the price on one day, smoothing out spikes and dips — useful when your real exposure is to an average cost or rate.
concept.mechanics: An average-price call pays max(A - K, 0), where A is the average of the underlying over the contracted fixing schedule (daily, weekly, monthly; arithmetic or geometric); average-strike variants use A as the strike. Averaging reduces volatility of the payoff determinant, so Asian options are generally cheaper than comparable vanillas, and they hedge exposures to average prices, such as monthly commodity purchases.
concept.formula: Average-price call payoff = max(A - K, 0) with A = (1/n) x sum of S_i over the n fixings (arithmetic) or A = (product of S_i)^(1/n) (geometric).
concept.failure_modes: Averaging mutes exactly the extreme moves an option buyer may want to capture; a late price spike barely moves the payoff. Arithmetic-average Asians have no simple closed-form price under standard models, and contracts referencing few fixings are vulnerable to fixing-window manipulation.
concept.misconceptions: That the lower premium makes an Asian option a better deal — the discount reflects a genuinely smaller payoff distribution. Also, the 'average' is of prices on scheduled fixing dates, not of every traded price.
concept.example: An airline buys a 12-month average-price call on monthly jet fuel fixings to cap its average annual fuel cost rather than any single month's price.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
